newsitem.title: FRANCE: French leftists confident as poll campaign ends.
newsitem.headline: French leftists confident as poll campaign ends.

text.p: French Socialist and Communist leaders paraded together on Friday, the last day of campaigning for Sunday's crucial, tight parliamentary election runoff, despite strains within their joint challenge to the ruling centre-right.

Socialist Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue were mobbed by reporters as they toured a poor north Paris suburb and held private talks after Hue had highlighted differences within a left-wing opposition which sounded increasingly confident.
The stock market was edgy but steady on Friday after the CAC-40 index had shed more than six percent earlier this week on prospects of a left-wing victory.
"It is impossible to imagine a Left that would not quickly launch a series of (left-wing) measures..." Hue said in a television interview.

He spelled out terms for joining a possible Socialist-led government, including demands for pay rises and new taxes on investment earnings, anathema to the ruling coalition which has increasingly angled its campaign against the "perils of a Communist return to power".

The centre-right, outpolled by the combined left in the first round, pinned its final hopes on its own leadership duo, socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer ex-finance minister Alain Madelin.

Seguin was hastily anointed as the right's new campaign leader after unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe took the blame for last Sunday's poll debacle and said he would quit after the runoff, whatever the result.
The left's first-round upset forced Chirac to contemplate the prospect of sharing power with a left-wing government in an arrangement known in France as "cohabitation".

Seguin made a rousing speech by video-link to the closing conservative rally in Paris on Thursday night, but gave no indication of what his policies would be if he became prime minister. Instead he focused on attacking the Socialists' government record in the 1980s and early 1990s.

The last stretch of the campaign was marred by violence as two people, including a Socialist parliamentary candidate, were injured when anti-racist militants hurled eggs at Jean-Marie Le Pen and clashed with militants of his far-right National Front.
Le Pen was campaigning for his daughter Marie Caroline Le Pen in the troubled Paris suburb of Mantes-la-Jolie.
There was another clash in the southern town of Orange on Thursday night and police said two Front militants were slightly injured in a blaze set by arsonists at the local Front office.
Jospin, 59, also campaigned near Paris with his other ally, Greens leader Dominique Voynet, who said the ecologists, like the Communists, were pondering whether to join the cabinet if the left wins.
Alain Bocquet, Communist floor leader in the outgoing National Assembly, said his party would decide on Monday whether to join a cabinet after consulting party members.
He said the Communists would be loyal allies "whether we participate in a government or whether we support it without participating".
The two campaign allies have bickered before over European monetary union, which the Communists oppose but the Socialists generally favour.
Jospin aides said he would accept no conditions from his Communist allies, and would demand that they commit themselves to a lasting participation in the cabinet if they decided to join.

Some analysts said Hue's militant demands could be a ploy to suggest the Communists were unlikely to join a left-wing cabinet. Their absence could be an incentive to hesitant voters to cast ballots for a more reassuring-looking left, which sounds increasingly confident of victory.
Socialists were already debating draft cabinet lists and weighing legislative strategy should they take power.
An elated Jospin said on Thursday night the French left was on the brink of a victory which would stun and cheer Europe a month after Labour's victory in Britain.
"This evening, I am telling you, we can win on Sunday," Jospin told cheering supporters in the northern town of Lille.
Chirac called the election 10 months early to seek a new five-year lease for his centre-right government and a "new elan" for France as it prepares to join a single European currency.
But he badly misjudged voters' dismay at record 12.8 percent unemployment and government austerity programmes adopted to help France qualify for the euro common currency.
